To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) process goals lead to higher self-efficacy and satisfaction with performance than outcome goals, (2) process goals lead students to attribute success and failure to more internal and stable causes than outcome goals, and (3) self-evaluation leads students to attribute success to more internal and unstable causes than not self-evaluating their work.

(a) process goal setting is a more powerful strategy than outcome goal setting in terms of its impact on student skill acquisition; (b) process goal setting, but not outcome goal setting, is more beneficial for students who do not engage in self-evaluation; (c) self-evaluation is beneficial for students who are given outcome, but not process, goal instructions; and (d) organizational signals do not influence students' skill acquisition, self-efficacious beliefs, or satisfaction with their performance

(a) goal setting had an impact on students' self-efficiency and satisfaction with their performance; (b) self-evaluation had an impact on skill acquisition and satisfaction; and (c) goal setting and self-evaluation had no impact on students' attributions for success or lack of it.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of self-regulated learners and the ways in which they learn.
the effects of goal setting and self-evaluation on student performance in a complex, computer-based learning environment.
the effects of goal setting, self-evaluation, and organizational signals on the acquisition of procedural skills and a variety of affect-related outcomes, including self-efficacy and satisfaction.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
goal setting and self-evaluation are important for self-regulated learning, whereas organizational signals are not.
students who set goals for themselves and who self-evaluate their performance will acquire the skill more effectively than those who do not set goals and/or evaluate their own performance.
students who were given process goals and were directed to self-evaluation performed better than students who were given outcome goals and were not directed to evaluate their work.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
process goals, self-evaluation, and the absence of organizational signals are all beneficial to the learning of procedural skills.
process goal setting and self-evaluation are important components of a self-regulated learning environment.
the use of process goals and self-evaluation can help students to develop self-regulatory strategies, which can in turn enhance their ability to learn.
The main takeaway from our work is that
students who are given process goals and who are encouraged to engage in self-evaluation will be more successful than those who are not.
the process of self-regulated learning is not a single, linear process but rather an iterative process that involves the interplay of multiple variables.
the process of setting a goal, and the process of self-evaluating one's performance, can be more important than the specific goal or self-evaluation that is set.
